newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Midwest hog plants trim kills on weak margins.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Midwest hog plants trim kills on weak margins.

text.p: Many U.S. Midwest hog plants on Monday reduced slaughter operations in efforts to mend operating margins, company and industry sources said.
"We are reducing operating hours until the supply and demand situation comes back into line," said Mark Klein, spokesman for Excel Corp, a division of Cargill Inc.
Klein declined to comment on how much shifts would be reduced or for how long, but did say all three of Excel's pork plants would be affected.
Excel operates pork plants in Ottumwa, Iowa; Beardstown, Ill., and Marshall, Mo.
Industry sources estimated reductions at the various companies' plants would be about one to two hours per shift on a day-to-day basis at plants where operations were trimmed.
ConAgra Inc also planned slaughter cutbacks at its Swift and Co pork plants in Marshalltown, Iowa and Worthington, Minn., said K.T. Miller, ConAgra spokeswoman.

Farmland Industries reportedly shaved operating hours at its Farmland Foods pork plants in Denison, Iowa, Crete, Neb., and Monomuth Ill., a source close to the company said. Company officials were unavailable for comment.

Operations at John Morrell and Co., a subsidiary of Smithfield Foods were not expected to be trimmed, a company source who asked not to be identified, said. Morrell operates plants in Sioux Falls, S.D., and Sioux City, Iowa.
IBP Inc spokesman Gary Mickelson said he had no immediate information regarding operating hours at IBP's pork plants.
Officials at other pork plants were either unavailable for comment or did not have current information about operating schedules.

Cash hog prices in direct trade last week climbed $2.50 to $3.00 per cwt, with plants in interior Iowa and southern Minnesota paying up to $57.50 for hogs delivered to plants, USDA reported. The gains last week were tied to seasonally tight supplies, industry sources said. Also, farmers in some areas were preoccupied with spring fieldwork and lacked time to sell hogs.
Packer margins were eroded by the failure of pork prices to climb as quickly as hog prices, they said.
Hog slaughter Monday was estimated at 291,000 head, well below 336,000 a week ago and 343,000 a year ago, USDA reported.
